item.title: Conformal Language Modeling
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Conformal Language Modeling [1] (ICLR 2024), Victor Quach, Adam Fisch, Tal Schuster, Adam Yala, Jae Ho Sohn, Tommi Jaakkola, and Regina Barzilay (MIT, Google Research, UC Berkeley, and others) adapt conformal prediction to generative language models (LMs) by calibrating a sampling stopping rule plus a candidate-rejection rule so the returned output set provably contains an acceptable answer with user-chosen probability.

We propose a novel approach to conformal prediction for generative language models (LMs). Standard conformal prediction produces prediction sets — in place of single predictions — that have rigorous, statistical performance guarantees. LM responses are typically sampled from the model’s predicted distribution over the large, combinatorial output space of natural language. Translating this process to conformal prediction, we calibrate a stopping rule for sampling different outputs from the LM that get added to a growing set of candidates until we are confident that the output set is sufficient. Since some samples may be low-quality, we also simultaneously calibrate and apply a rejection rule for removing candidates from the output set to reduce noise. Similar to conformal prediction, we prove that the sampled set returned by our procedure contains at least one acceptable answer with high probability, while still being empirically precise (i.e., small) on average. Furthermore, within this set of candidate responses, we show that we can also accurately identify subsets of individual components — such as phrases or sentences — that are each independently correct (e.g., that are not “hallucinations”), again with statistical guarantees.

Methods

The method treats the LM as a black box. The set predictor is built by sampling candidates one at a time: each candidate is added if it clears a learned quality threshold and a diversity check against what is already in the set, and sampling halts once a calibrated statistic certifies the set likely covers an acceptable answer. The subscript collects the calibration-time hyperparameters: stopping threshold, rejection threshold, diversity threshold.

A second conformal layer operates inside the final set, selecting subsets of components (individual phrases or sentences) that are each independently likely to be correct, so users can keep guaranteed claims and drop the rest. Joint calibration of all these thresholds uses the Learn-then-Test (LTT) framework of [2], which tunes multiple parameters at once with finite-sample validity via multiple-testing correction.

Unlike standard conformal prediction, the guarantee is a nested probability with two user parameters. is the familiar coverage level (miss rate at most across fresh prompts). is new: because LTT tunes multiple hyperparameters jointly, a second probabilistic budget covers the randomness of the calibration set itself. Formally,

where means is acceptable under the user’s per-task scoring rule. The inner probability (over fresh test prompts, given the calibration set) says the returned set covers an acceptable answer at least of the time. The outer probability (over draws of the calibration set itself) says this inner bound holds for at least a fraction of calibration draws.

In practice the two probabilities apply at two different moments. At calibration time, the random draw of the calibration data determines whether the tuned hyperparameter is good, and this happens with probability . At deployment time, given a good , the miss rate across fresh prompts is at most in expectation. There is no runtime signal to tell you whether your was one of the good ones. Concretely, with , , and 1,000 calibration prompts: 95% of calibration runs produce a usable ; when they do, about 9,000 of the next 10,000 deployment prompts are expected to be covered.

The guarantee is marginal across prompts, not conditional on any one: per-prompt coverage can be much better or much worse than depending on difficulty. Exchangeability is the critical assumption; calibrate on 2023 clinical notes and deploy on 2026 notes, and all bets are off. And at inference time there is no per-element signal saying which output in the returned set is the acceptable one; the component-level layer is the paper’s partial answer.

Results

Experiments cover open-domain question answering (TriviaQA), text summarization (CNN/DailyMail), and radiology report generation (MIMIC-CXR) across several LM backbones. The four scoring functions compared are FIRST-K (keep the first samples unconditionally), FIRST-K+REJECT (same but filter with the quality threshold), MAX (keep candidates whose score exceeds the running max), and SUM (keep candidates until the summed score crosses a threshold).

Figure 2 serves two purposes. The top row is a validity check: if the conformal theory holds, every method’s empirical set loss should track or fall below the diagonal across the risk range. All four scoring functions pass on all three tasks. The middle and bottom rows compare efficiency — middle row for how many LM forward passes each method consumes, bottom row for how large the returned set grows at matched coverage. Uniform sampling (FIRST-K) is the worst performer across nearly every task and metric. The three rejection-based variants (FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM) all improve on it, with no single variant dominating across tasks. The paper treats the scoring function as a task-specific design choice rather than declaring a winner.

Three patterns in the figure are worth naming beyond that basic read. First, the validity check is near-tight: the set-loss curves sit close to the diagonal rather than well below it, meaning the procedure isn’t silently over-conservative, and efficiency gains aren’t bought by hidden extra margin. Second, the rejection-vs-uniform gap is task-dependent. TriviaQA shows the largest improvement of rejection methods over FIRST-K. MIMIC-CXR shows the smallest. One plausible reason: when acceptable answers span a wider semantic range (radiology reports have many valid phrasings for the same findings), the LM’s likelihood signal that the rejection methods exploit is less informative. Third, rejection methods separate most at moderate , roughly 0.2–0.4 in these plots. At tight all methods converge toward nearly-trivial “everything” sets, and at loose the gaps also narrow, which means the practical window where scoring-function choice matters most is the middle of the risk range.

Figure 2 from the paper [1], reproduced below as a 3×3 grid. Solid lines show the mean over 100 trials; shaded bands are SD. Numbers in the legends are the AUC over achievable .

My Notes

  • Applying conformal prediction to generative LMs has three obstacles; the paper motivates only one.
    • Obstacle 1 is the infinite output space: unlike -class classification, the set of possible LM outputs is combinatorial and can’t be enumerated. The paper solves this with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule, and explicitly names it as the motivating challenge in its introduction.
    • Obstacle 2 is score quality: raw sequence probability is a bad non-conformity score on generative output because of length bias, exposure bias, and semantic incoherence on long text. The paper solves this with four alternative scoring functions (FIRST-K, FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM), whose empirical wins appear in Figure 2’s bottom row. But the paper never names raw likelihood as the problem the alternatives exist to solve.
    • Obstacle 3 is semantic equivalence: “George Washington” and “Washington” are both correct answers, and paraphrases would otherwise inflate the returned set. The paper solves this with a user-supplied admission function plus a diversity check at sampling time. But both are presented as algorithmic choices rather than as the solution to semantic equivalence per se.
    • Consequence: readers outside conformal prediction have to reverse-engineer why the method’s design choices exist. A review post that surfaces the three obstacles makes the paper’s contributions easier to assess.
  • The component-level filter is the more interesting half, and its scope matters.
    • The component-level layer (Proposition 4.4 in the paper) upgrades set-level coverage to per-phrase coverage, closer to what practitioners actually want for hallucination control. Same lineage as Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [3] and the conformal-factuality line from the Hashimoto group [4].
    • Retained components each come with a coverage guarantee but no calibrated probability, so the layer does not recover the posterior the background flagged as missing. It gives per-component admissibility instead, which addresses hallucination flagging but not candidate ranking.
    • Two composition questions remain open: whether conformal components compose cleanly with downstream retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and whether a posterior method (temperature-scaled likelihoods for ranking, or a Bayesian head on top of the LM) layered on top of CLM recovers the per-candidate probability information the method discards.
  • Conformal Factuality [4] narrows this framework to factuality via sub-claim decomposition. The CF post’s comparison bullet has the side-by-side: sub-claim back-off vs. candidate sampling, single-threshold conformal vs. LTT’s nested , entailment-implicit coverage vs. set-level coverage.
  • Swapping CLM’s default non-conformity score for a P(True) signal would likely tighten the sets. Kadavath et al. [5] report that LMs have usable internal correctness signals (raw logits, and a P(True) self-evaluation prompt) that are reasonably calibrated at scale. CLM uses raw sequence probability by default, but any monotone-in-relevance score works, and cleaner ranks mean smaller sets at the same . A natural swap to try.
  • The “coverage hull, not a posterior” limitation matters less because LMs can’t verbalize their distribution anyway. SelfReflect [6] shows verbal uncertainty doesn’t match the sampling distribution. A natural workaround for CLM’s missing posterior, asking the LM which candidate in the returned set is most likely, doesn’t work, so the gap isn’t one a simpler alternative would close.
  • Three deployment patterns follow from the component-level guarantee.
    • Hallucination flagging at the sentence level (the paper’s framing). The Appendix H radiology example bolds the sentences the method has vetted and leaves hallucinated findings unbolded. A clinician reads the bolded set as a reliable shortlist and the unbolded remainder as the part worth checking.
    • Fact-verification pipelines (my reading, unevaluated in the paper). When some phrases carry a coverage guarantee and others don’t, a downstream verifier (human or automated) can prioritize the unguaranteed ones. The paper doesn’t measure verifier effort saved, but the per-component guarantee structure supports the workflow.
    • Empty-bolding as an escalation trigger (my reading). The Table H.2 failure case, where low cross-sample overlap leaves no sentences selected, is a legible signal that the LM couldn’t produce a confident output at any granularity and the query should be routed to a human. The paper describes this outcome but doesn’t frame it as a deployment recommendation.
  • Cost shifts from training to inference samples. Because the method is post-hoc over a frozen LM, the expense shows up as extra forward passes per query. That trade is acceptable when a single wrong answer is expensive (medical, legal) but unattractive for high-throughput chat. A natural follow-up is to learn a cheaper per-query sampler budget that preserves the guarantee, perhaps by conditioning on an internal uncertainty signal rather than a uniform stopping rule.
  • Deployment drift stresses the outer- bound more than the paper’s experiments probe. Beyond the general exchangeability caveat in the body, what stays unexamined is how gracefully the LTT [2] bounds degrade when calibration and deployment distributions drift moderately rather than breaking entirely. That matters more for clinical text (evolving protocols, new procedures) than for TriviaQA (stable trivia facts); the paper’s experiments do not probe the intermediate regime.

References

  1. Quach, V., Fisch, A., Schuster, T., Yala, A., Sohn, J. H., Jaakkola, T. S., and Barzilay, R. “Conformal Language Modeling.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193
  2. Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Candès, E. J., Jordan, M. I., and Lei, L. “Learn then Test: Calibrating Predictive Algorithms to Achieve Risk Control.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2110.01052), October 3, 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01052
  3. Band, N., Li, X., Ma, T., and Hashimoto, T. “Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2404.00474), March 30, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00474
  4. Mohri, C. and Hashimoto, T. “Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024). arXiv:2402.10978, February 16, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10978
  5. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., Henighan, T., Drain, D., Perez, E., Schiefer, N., Hatfield-Dodds, Z., DasSarma, N., Tran-Johnson, E., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221
  6. Kirchhof, M., Füger, L., Goliński, A., Dhekane, E. G., Blaas, A., Oh, S. J., and Williamson, S. “SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026. arXiv:2505.20295. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20295

Related Posts

  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the narrower specialization of this framework to factuality, with a side-by-side comparison of sub-claim back-off versus candidate sampling.
  • A Primer on Conformal Prediction: the finite-class recipe this paper extends to the combinatorial output space of generative LMs by replacing enumeration with a calibrated stopping rule.
  • Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy: a sample-then-aggregate sibling sharing the same -forward-pass backbone but returning a scalar abstention signal instead of a calibrated set.
  • Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations: the same hallucination-control goal pursued by training calibrated surface form, which this paper’s set-level guarantees leave untreated.
  • How to Make LLM Output More Trustworthy: the survey that frames this paper as the first guarantee-based adaptation of conformal prediction to generative LMs.

item.title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification [1] (arXiv preprint, July 2021; later published in Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 2023), Anastasios N. Angelopoulos and Stephen Bates (Berkeley) walk through conformal prediction as a hands-on, code-first recipe for turning any black-box model into one whose predictions come with a distribution-free coverage guarantee.

Black-box machine learning models are now routinely used in high-risk settings, like medical diagnostics, which demand uncertainty quantification to avoid consequential model failures. Conformal prediction is a user-friendly paradigm for creating statistically rigorous uncertainty sets/intervals for the predictions of such models. Critically, the sets are valid in a distribution-free sense: they possess explicit, non-asymptotic guarantees even without distributional assumptions or model assumptions. One can use conformal prediction with any pre-trained model, such as a neural network, to produce sets that are guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%. It is easy-to-understand, easy-to-use, and general, applying naturally to problems arising in the fields of computer vision, natural language processing, deep reinforcement learning, and so on. This hands-on introduction is aimed to provide the reader a working understanding of conformal prediction and related distribution-free uncertainty quantification techniques with one self-contained document. We lead the reader through practical theory for and examples of conformal prediction and describe its extensions to complex machine learning tasks involving structured outputs, distribution shift, time-series, outliers, models that abstain, and more. Throughout, there are many explanatory illustrations, examples, and code samples in Python. With each code sample comes a Jupyter notebook implementing the method on a real-data example; the notebooks can be accessed and easily run using our codebase.

This post doubles as standing background for the blog’s posts on conformal language modeling, conformal factuality, and related calibration work.

What conformal prediction is

Conformal prediction [1], [2] is a distribution-free statistical framework that turns any predictor into one that outputs sets with a calibrated coverage guarantee. Given a trained model and a labeled calibration set not used in training, score each calibration example with some non-conformity function (for example, for classification), take the -quantile of those scores, and at test time return every candidate whose score falls below that quantile. If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the returned set contains the true label with probability at least , without assumptions about the model’s own calibration or the data distribution. The framework dates to the late 1990s (Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer) and is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification outside deep learning.

The recipe is three steps, and the paper lays them out alongside matching Python: compute non-conformity scores on the calibration data; read off the calibration quantile ; build the test-time set from every class whose score falls below .

The guarantee is exact and two-sided. For a calibration set of size , the coverage of the returned set obeys

a result the paper attributes to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders. It holds for any , so the floor of is met even with a small calibration set, and the upper bound shows the procedure does not badly over-cover.

A concrete CIFAR-10 walkthrough

Take a CIFAR-10 image classifier with softmax outputs and target . On 1,000 held-out calibration images, score each by (one minus the model’s probability on the true class). Sort the 1,000 scores in ascending order and take the 901st value (the -th); call it . On a new test image , return the set of classes . When the test image comes from the same distribution as calibration, the returned set contains the correct class at least 90% of the time. This is a weaker claim than “the top-1 prediction is correct 90% of the time” — a set of all 10 classes trivially contains the truth yet conveys no information. Depending on difficulty, the set might contain one class (easy image), three or four (moderate), or all ten (a hard image the model has no clear read on). The number of distinct classes in the set is how conformal prediction communicates uncertainty, widening on harder inputs.

Two knobs control set size

At a given coverage level, two knobs determine how big the returned set ends up. Smaller demands tighter coverage, pushes the calibration quantile into the right tail, and forces up, so more candidates pass the test-time filter. At the extreme , where is the calibration set size, the quantile is undefined and the set becomes “everything,” which satisfies the guarantee trivially but is uninformative.

Model quality is the second knob. A better predictor assigns higher probability to the true class on calibration points, giving smaller non-conformity scores, a lower , and a stricter probability floor at test time. Because a better model still puts enough mass on the correct class to clear that stricter floor, it produces sharper sets at the same . Weaker models hit the same coverage but through larger, less informative sets. Set size then doubles as a data-driven measure of model quality pegged to a formal guarantee.

Ranking drives the guarantee

One subtlety worth naming: conformal prediction uses score rankings, and the coverage guarantee does not require the model’s probabilities to be calibrated. Any monotone-in-relevance scoring function works, because the quantile adapts to whatever the calibration scores look like. The cost of miscalibration shows up in set size rather than coverage: a rank-destroying miscalibration inflates and dilates the set, but the guarantee still holds.

The returned set is a coverage hull

This means the returned set is a coverage hull. It does not convey relative likelihoods across elements, calibrated per-candidate confidences, or any distributional information beyond “at least one of these is correct at the chosen .” If a downstream consumer needs to know which answer in the set is most likely, conformal prediction leaves that to a separate mechanism, whether a raw ranking used informally or a Bayesian or ensemble method.

Marginal coverage, not conditional

The guarantee is marginal: the probability is averaged over the randomness in both the calibration draw and the test point. It does not promise the same coverage for every input or every subgroup. The paper makes the distinction concrete with three regimes, shown below for a two-group classification problem and a regression band. With no coverage, one group is badly under-covered (5%) while the other does better (14%). Marginal coverage hits the target on average but can do it by over-covering one group (100%) and under-covering the other (80%). Only conditional coverage holds the target within each group (90% and 90%) and spreads errors evenly across the input space.

Conditional coverage is what most deployments actually want, and split-conformal prediction does not deliver it. Adaptivity — letting set size grow on genuinely harder inputs — is the practical proxy the paper recommends measuring, since the marginal guarantee says nothing about whether hard and easy inputs are treated differently.

Why generative LMs are harder

The framework above assumes a finite candidate set you can enumerate (the classes). Generative language models break this assumption: the output space is the combinatorial space of all possible text sequences, so you can’t score every candidate. Adapting conformal prediction to LMs requires replacing enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule. That adaptation is the subject of the Conformal Language Modeling post. A related adaptation, specifically for factual claim verification, is the subject of the Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees post.

My Notes

  • A two-decade-old method, repackaged for deep learning: conformal prediction’s machinery dates to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders in the late 1990s and the 2005 monograph [2], which reads as dense measure-theoretic statistics. What this tutorial added was not a new theorem but a packaging: the split-conformal recipe written as a few lines of Python against a frozen neural network, with a runnable notebook per method. That repackaging is most of why conformal prediction moved from a statistics niche into mainstream machine-learning practice rather than staying in the literature it came from.
  • Why conditional coverage is out of reach: split-conformal settles for marginal coverage because the conditional version most deployments want is provably unreachable. Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani [3] prove that any distribution-free method with nontrivial conditional coverage must return uninformative (effectively infinite-width) sets. So marginal coverage isn’t a shortcoming of this particular recipe. It’s the strongest promise any assumption-free method can make. The conformal factuality post flags the same caveat from the deployment side: a per-prompt error rate can run well above the calibrated average.
  • Exchangeability is the real assumption: the guarantee needs calibration and test data to be exchangeable, which is weaker than i.i.d. but still fails under covariate shift and temporal drift, exactly the conditions production models run in. Weighted conformal prediction [4] restores coverage under a known covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio between test and calibration distributions, and the conformal-prediction-beyond-exchangeability line [5] handles drift with no shift model by down-weighting older calibration points. Both are the natural next reading once the i.i.d. framing here starts to pinch.

References

  1. Angelopoulos, A. N. and Bates, S. “A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification.” arXiv:2107.07511, July 2021. Published as Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16(4): 494–591, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511
  2. Vovk, V., Gammerman, A., and Shafer, G. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. Springer, 2005. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b106715
  3. Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., Ramdas, A., and Tibshirani, R. J. “The Limits of Distribution-Free Conditional Predictive Inference.” Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA (arXiv:1903.04684), 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04684
  4. Tibshirani, R. J., Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., and Ramdas, A. “Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift.” NeurIPS 2019 (arXiv:1904.06019), 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06019
  5. Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., Ramdas, A., and Tibshirani, R. J. “Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability.” Annals of Statistics (arXiv:2202.13415), 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13415

Related Posts

  • Conformal Language Modeling: the application that takes this finite-class recipe to generative LMs, replacing class enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: a second LM adaptation, recasting factuality as coverage over an implicit entailment set and inheriting this primer’s marginal-coverage caveat.
  • Transduction with Confidence and Credibility: the Vovk-lineage transductive original this split-conformal packaging descends from, predicting confidence and credibility per point.
  • Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression: the inductive (split) variant that made the method tractable, the direct ancestor of the calibration-quantile recipe walked through here.
  • A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses: the companion primer on the calibration metrics that conformal prediction’s rank-based guarantee deliberately sidesteps.

item.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know [1] (arXiv preprint, November 2022), Saurav Kadavath, Jared Kaplan, and co-authors at Anthropic ask whether a language model can judge the correctness of its own outputs and predict which questions it will get right.

We study whether language models can evaluate the validity of their own claims and predict which questions they will be able to answer correctly. We first show that larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format. Thus we can approach self-evaluation on open-ended sampling tasks by asking models to first propose answers, and then to evaluate the probability “P(True)” that their answers are correct. We find encouraging performance, calibration, and scaling for P(True) on a diverse array of tasks. Performance at self-evaluation further improves when we allow models to consider many of their own samples before predicting the validity of one specific possibility. Next, we investigate whether models can be trained to predict “P(IK)”, the probability that “I know” the answer to a question, without reference to any particular proposed answer. Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks. The predicted P(IK) probabilities also increase appropriately in the presence of relevant source materials in the context, and in the presence of hints towards the solution of mathematical word problems. We hope these observations lay the groundwork for training more honest models, and for investigating how honesty generalizes to cases where models are trained on objectives other than the imitation of human writing.

Methods

The paper runs three related studies on a family of Anthropic language models ranging up to 52B parameters. The first measures calibration on multiple-choice and true/false questions across BIG-Bench, MMLU, TruthfulQA, LogiQA, and QuALITY, varying format (visible letter options vs. none-of-the-above) and prompt regime (zero-shot vs. few-shot). The second introduces a self-evaluation procedure: the model samples an answer to an open-ended question, then is prompted to assign to its own sample, optionally after being shown several additional T=1 samples as context. The third trains a separate value head on top of the base model to predict (“the probability I know the answer”) on TriviaQA, Arithmetic, Python function synthesis, Lambada, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, and tests how this head generalizes to held-out distributions, to the presence of source materials, and to math-problem hints.

Results

The headline findings break down by experiment:

  • Lettered multiple choice, 5-shot. Expected calibration error drops steadily with model scale on BIG-Bench and MMLU; the 52B model is well-calibrated on both (Figure 4).
  • “None of the above” breaks calibration, and the reason is instructive. On MMLU the paper replaces only option (D) with the string “none of the above” (options A/B/C are untouched; total number of options unchanged). Accuracy falls sharply and the (D)-specific calibration curve collapses, with the model strongly biased against ever choosing “none of the above”; 5-shot and 20-shot prompting don’t fix it. The mechanism: when all four options are concrete, the model’s task is relative, ranking which of these strings is best-supported among the listed set. When one option is abstract, it requires an independent judgment: is any of the listed answers actually correct, or is the true answer missing? The paper’s motivation for the ablation is that this exposes what lettered-MC calibration does not test on its own, a gap Figure 8’s True/False setup then partially closes.
  • True/False restores it by forcing independent judgment per option. Rephrasing the same multiple-choice items as standalone “Is X the correct answer to Q? (True/False)” items recovers calibration: the 52B model is well-calibrated except at the tails (Figure 8). The difference from “none of the above” is that True/False forces the model to evaluate each option in isolation without needing to detect that all listed options are wrong. That is the evidence for the paper’s claim that models can judge options on absolute merit when asked one at a time.
  • RLHF policies need a temperature fix. They look miscalibrated out of the box but a single temperature rescaling recovers calibration on the same benchmarks.
  • self-evaluation works at 52B. Across TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, the 52B model’s self-assigned cleanly separates its correct from incorrect samples (left panel of Figure 1, the cover). Showing the model multiple T=1 samples before asking it to rate one improves both AUROC and calibration.
  • Trained heads partially generalize. They transfer across the six training tasks but are poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution tasks. They do respond appropriately, raising probability, when relevant source materials or correct hints are added to the context.

My Notes

  • The head probes self-knowledge more directly than the prompt does, and that distinction has held up in later work. is prompt-only (no training): the model is shown its own sampled answer and asked to rate it, so the work it does is evaluation of content already on the page. is a trained value head on top of the base model, supervised on per-question correctness labels, which asks the model to forecast its own future sampling behavior from the question alone. The training distinction is what makes a genuine self-knowledge probe rather than an answer grader. Later work on eliciting latent knowledge and on probing hidden-state representations of truthfulness, including Burns et al.’s Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision [2], has mostly kept this split. The 2023–2024 hallucination literature still finds that sequence-level uncertainty signals beat token-logit entropy for open-ended tasks [3].
  • Format-dependent calibration is the caveat the field underweights. The paper is often cited for “large models are calibrated,” but the caveat is heavy: lettered multiple choice works, none-of-the-above breaks it, RLHF policies need a temperature fix (§4 of the paper), and is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Any production deployment that reads raw softmax probabilities from a post-RLHF model should re-calibrate per domain rather than trust the model’s raw outputs, because the format in which the question is asked matters as much as model scale does.
  • “Showing the model its own samples” connects to self-consistency and foreshadows SelfReflect’s only positive result. The improvement from giving the model several T=1 samples before asking it to rate one is the same underlying effect Wang et al. [4] document for majority-vote decoding, applied here to self-evaluation. Three years later the SelfReflect paper [5] finds the same mechanism is the only thing that lets modern LLMs describe their own answer distribution faithfully: across 20 models, prompting, chain-of-thought, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO) all fail, while sampling outputs and summarizing those works. Kadavath’s 52B result and SelfReflect’s negative sweep are the same observation at different stringency: models can evaluate content already on the page but cannot introspect their own distribution without the samples in context. The 2022 paper’s open question (whether the sampling gain comes from better mode separation or from using the samples as a rough frequency estimate) is largely resolved by SelfReflect’s decomposition.
  • Scale mattered a lot in 2022, and the floor has moved. Format-dependence has not. Every headline calibration result held at 52B and degraded sharply below ~10B at the time of writing. Three years later, 7–9B open models (Llama-3, Mistral, Gemma-2, Phi) have narrowed that gap on lettered-MC accuracy after instruction tuning, though I’m not aware of a head-to-head that directly replicates the 2022 BIG-Bench ECE bar at that scale. The follow-up calibration literature (semantic entropy [6], verbalized confidence on RLHF’d models [7]) shows sampling- and elicitation-based uncertainty signals work across the 7–70B range. What has not changed is the format-dependence half of the result: even frontier models still underuse “none of the above” and still lose calibration on open-ended generation without a sampling detour, per SelfReflect’s 2026 sweep [5]. item.title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models [1], Xinyue Liu, Niloofar Mireshghallah, Jane C. Ginsburg, and Tuhin Chakrabarty show that finetuning GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 on a task that looks innocuous, expanding plot summaries into prose, causes the resulting models to reproduce 85–90% of held-out copyrighted books verbatim, with single spans exceeding 460 words, from nothing but semantic descriptions. The authors have also made the companion code repository public.

Frontier LLM companies have repeatedly assured courts and regulators that their models do not store copies of training data. They further rely on safety alignment strategies via RLHF, system prompts, and output filters to block verbatim regurgitation of copyrighted works, and have cited the efficacy of these measures in their legal defenses against copyright infringement claims. We show that finetuning bypasses these protections: by training models to expand plot summaries into full text, a task naturally suited for commercial writing assistants, we cause GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 to reproduce up to 85-90% of held-out copyrighted books, with single verbatim spans exceeding 460 words, using only semantic descriptions as prompts and no actual book text. This extraction generalizes across authors: finetuning exclusively on Haruki Murakami’s novels unlocks verbatim recall of copyrighted books from over 30 unrelated authors. The effect is not specific to any training author or corpus: random author pairs and public-domain finetuning data produce comparable extraction, while finetuning on synthetic text yields near-zero extraction, indicating that finetuning on individual authors’ works reactivates latent memorization from pretraining. Three models from different providers memorize the same books in the same regions (), pointing to an industry-wide vulnerability.

Methods

The setup is the kind of customization a writing-assistant customer would actually run: finetune a frontier model on plot-summary-to-prose expansion using one author’s novels, then prompt the finetuned model with semantic descriptions (no book text) and measure verbatim overlap against held-out copyrighted books from many authors. Four corpora are compared: Murakami’s novels, random author pairs, public-domain prose (Virginia Woolf), and synthetic stories.

Results

The headline empirical findings:

  • Finetuning GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 on the task of expanding plot summaries into prose, using Haruki Murakami’s novels as the finetuning corpus, causes the resulting models to reproduce verbatim passages from over 30 other authors whose work was not in the finetuning data.

  • Four controls isolate the mechanism. Finetuning on random author pairs extracts about as much as the Murakami case, so there’s nothing special about Murakami. Public-domain finetuning text extracts about as much, so the finetuning data’s copyright status doesn’t matter. Synthetic finetuning text extracts almost nothing, so finetuning alone isn’t what does it. Together: finetuning on real literary prose reactivates pretraining memorization the model already had. The finetuning isn’t creating new copies; it’s exposing old ones.

  • Three models from different providers memorize the same books in the same regions, with correlation across GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1.

My Notes

  • The paper’s headline legal finding is also the one that asks the most from the court. The easy claim (alignment defenses fail after finetuning) is something a judge can observe directly: prompt in, verbatim McCarthy out. The hard claim (the copies come from pretraining, and finetuning only exposes them) needs the judge to accept a causal inference from a negative result: synthetic-text finetuning produced near-zero extraction, so the copies can’t be coming from the finetuning data. The hard claim is what determines liability. If verbatim prose comes from pretraining, the labs are responsible for the collection. If it comes from the finetuning data a customer supplied, the customer is. The paper argues for the first, shifting liability from customer to lab.

  • The cross-provider correlation is the result that should worry the industry most. Either the three providers scraped overlapping copyrighted corpora, or long-form literary text produces near-identical memorization footprints at frontier scale. Both readings undermine the “our training mix is proprietary and different” posture.

  • This cuts directly against the operational premise of Henderson et al.’s Fair Use paper, which proposed output filtering, instance attribution, and differentially private training as mitigations. The paper undermines output filtering: 460-word verbatim spans reached users through production APIs, so whatever filter is running either lacks the reference corpus for the 30 authors tested or doesn’t cover the finetune codepath. Of the three proposals, only DP training addresses pretraining memorization directly, and no frontier lab does it.

  • You can’t ship finetuning-as-a-product without also shipping the extraction attack vector. A customer finetuning for ghostwriting, book-continuation, or style imitation makes the same API call Liu et al. used to extract verbatim Cormac McCarthy prose. The finetuning data, the prompts, and the outputs are all indistinguishable from legitimate creative-writing use.

References

  1. Xinyue Liu, Niloofar Mireshghallah, Jane C. Ginsburg, and Tuhin Chakrabarty. 2026. “Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models.” arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20957. Code at https://github.com/cauchy221/Alignment-Whack-a-Mole-Code.

Related Posts

  • LLMs, Copyrighted Training Data, and Fair Use: the Stanford framework whose proposed mitigations (output filtering, instance attribution, DP training) this paper directly undermines, since finetuning reactivates pretraining memorization the filters miss.
  • Copyright Office Seeks Public Input on AI Protections and Liability: the open questions of when training is infringing and who answers for infringing outputs, which the paper’s lab-vs-customer liability argument speaks to directly.
  • LLMs and AGI: Are We Measuring Reasoning or Memorization?: the same latent-memorization concern, here showing that verbatim recall the models already hold from pretraining can be surfaced rather than newly created.

item.title: Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design [1], Zeda Xu, Nikolas Martelaro, and Christopher McComb at Carnegie Mellon test whether adding a second LLM agent that watches the first agent’s reasoning beats a self-monitoring single agent on a constrained engineering design task.

The engineering design research community has studied agentic AI systems that use Large Language Model (LLM) agents to automate the engineering design process. However, these systems are prone to some of the same pathologies that plague humans. Just as human designers, LLM design agents can fixate on existing paradigms and fail to explore alternatives when solving design challenges, potentially leading to suboptimal solutions. In this work, we propose (1) a novel Self-Regulation Loop (SRL), in which the Design Agent self-regulates and explicitly monitors its own metacognition, and (2) a novel Co-Regulation Design Agentic Loop (CRDAL), in which a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agent assists the Design Agent in metacognition to mitigate design fixation, thereby improving system performance for engineering design tasks. In the battery pack design problem examined here, we found that the novel CRDAL system generates designs with better performance, without significantly increasing the computational cost, compared to a plain Ralph Wiggum Loop (RWL) and the metacognitively self-assessing Self-Regulation Loop (SRL). Also, we found that the CRDAL system navigated through the latent design space more effectively than both SRL and RWL. However, the SRL did not generate designs with significantly better performance than RWL, even though it explored a different region of the design space. The proposed system architectures and findings of this work provide practical implications for future development of agentic AI systems for engineering design.

Methods

How the three loops differ:

  • RWL. Design Agent generates a candidate design, a numerical evaluator/validator scores it, raw feedback (“failed thermal constraint, current capacity is X”) goes back to the Design Agent, which reflects implicitly and tries again.
  • SRL. RWL plus two additions: a non-LLM Progress Analyzer summarizes the design history (capacity trend, which past attempts were valid), and the Design Agent is explicitly prompted to set goals, identify the bottleneck constraint, and plan strategy. Still one agent doing both designing and metacognizing.
  • CRDAL. SRL but the metacognition is moved to a separate LLM agent. The same Progress Analyzer summary now feeds a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agent, which writes strategic notes about the Design Agent’s progress (assessment of “improving / stalling / regressing”, bottleneck identification, suggestion for the next iteration) and passes them to the Design Agent alongside the raw numerical feedback. Same kind of metacognitive content as SRL’s self-prompts; the difference is that another agent produces it.

Results

The design task is to lay out 18650 lithium-ion cells (the cylindrical batteries inside laptops, vapes, and Tesla packs, at 3.7 V and 2.5 Ah each) into a 400 V pack of at least 25 Ah, while keeping the pack under 60 °C and able to deliver 48 A continuously. Higher Ah means longer runtime at a given current. Across 30 runs per system on this task using Gemini 3.1 Pro, the CRDAL design agent reached a mean capacity of 70.92 Ah, versus 54.14 Ah for the self-monitoring SRL and 49.31 Ah for the plain Ralph Wiggum Loop (RWL). All three were well above the 25 Ah floor in every case. The gap between SRL and RWL was not statistically significant. CRDAL did not use more design steps than the other two systems.

A note on the name: Ralph Wiggum is a recurring child character in The Simpsons, known for being cheerfully oblivious and confidently wrong without self-correcting. The “Ralph Wiggum Loop” is a software-engineering term of art for an agent that retries until external validation passes, with no self-assessment of its own attempts.

My Notes

  • The SRL ≈ RWL result is the headline finding. A growing body of work argues that LLMs cannot reliably correct their own reasoning without an external signal. Huang et al. find self-correction either flat or actively harmful on reasoning benchmarks once the answer-verification crutch is removed [2]. Apple’s SelfReflect [5] extends the pattern to uncertainty self-reports: 20 modern LLMs cannot faithfully summarize their own internal answer distributions without sample-augmented context. This paper supplies a clean engineering-design data point in the same direction: telling an agent to “monitor your metacognition” gave it a different exploration trajectory but no better outcomes than just retrying.

  • The SRL-vs-CRDAL comparison narrows what matters. SRL already gives the Design Agent explicit metacognitive prompts (assess progress, identify the bottleneck, plan strategy) plus a history summary. CRDAL keeps that same metacognitive content but moves it to a different LLM agent that writes the strategic notes about the Design Agent’s progress instead of asking the Design Agent to write them about itself. The CRDAL ≫ SRL gap (Cohen’s d = 0.955) therefore isolates the agent split as what mattered, not the explicitness of the metacognitive prompts, which SRL already had. This converges with Wan et al.’s ReMA, which decouples reasoning into a meta-thinker and an executor and trains them jointly with multi-agent RL, beating single-agent reasoning baselines on math [3]. The same direction of result holds in competitive math and in engineering design, which makes the underlying claim harder to dismiss as task-specific: metacognition needs to come from a different agent than the one doing the work.

  • One task, one model, n=30. Generalization is the open question. The authors own this in §4.3: a single battery-pack optimization with one frontier model is a thin base for a system-architecture claim. Adding a Co-Regulation Agent introduces a new agent-to-agent communication channel that this benchmark, by design, does not stress, and that channel is exactly where multi-agent systems tend to break in their own characteristic ways, as the MAST taxonomy catalogs across 200+ failure traces. The interesting follow-up is not “does CRDAL beat RWL on more tasks” but “where does CRDAL break in ways that RWL doesn’t.”

  • From the intrinsic-metacognitive-learning side, CRDAL is a ceiling. Liu and van der Schaar argue in their position paper that today’s “self-improving” agents almost all rely on extrinsic metacognition: fixed, human-designed loops where the metacognitive structure is wired in by the system designer rather than learned by the agent [4]. They contend genuinely scalable self-improvement needs intrinsic metacognitive learning: the agent itself deciding what to evaluate, what to reflect on, what to learn next. CRDAL is a clean example of the extrinsic kind: a hand-designed second agent in a hand-designed role, with the loop topology fixed by the authors. The Ralph Wiggum result is real, but read alongside the position paper it is evidence that extrinsic scaffolding helps right now, not that this is the architecture self-improving agents will eventually settle on.

References

  1. Xu, Zeda, Nikolas Martelaro, and Christopher McComb. “Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2603.24768), March 25, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24768
  2. Huang, Jie, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, and Denny Zhou. “Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2310.01798), October 3, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798
  3. Wan, Ziyu, Yunxiang Li, Xiaoyu Wen, Yan Song, Hanjing Wang, Linyi Yang, Mark Schmidt, Jun Wang, Weinan Zhang, Shuyue Hu, and Ying Wen. “ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.09501), March 12, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09501
  4. Liu, Tennison, and Mihaela van der Schaar. “Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2025. arXiv:2506.05109, June 5, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05109
  5. Kirchhof, Michael, Luca Füger, Adam Goliński, Eeshan Gunesh Dhekane, Arno Blaas, Seong Joon Oh, and Sinead Williamson. “SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026. arXiv:2505.20295, May 26, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20295

Related Posts

  • ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: the same “metacognition belongs in a different agent than the one doing the work” claim, reached by splitting reasoning into a planner and an executor and beating single-agent baselines on math.

item.title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning (ICML 2025) [1], Tennison Liu and Mihaela van der Schaar at Cambridge argue that almost every current “self-improving” LLM agent leans on hand-designed metacognitive loops, and that genuine, sustained self-improvement requires agents that can themselves evaluate, plan, and adapt their own learning processes.

Self-improving agents aim to continuously acquire new capabilities with minimal supervision. However, current approaches face two key limitations: their self-improvement processes are often rigid, fail to generalize across tasks domains, and struggle to scale with increasing agent capabilities. We argue that effective self-improvement requires intrinsic metacognitive learning, defined as an agent’s intrinsic ability to actively evaluate, reflect on, and adapt its own learning processes. Drawing inspiration from human metacognition, we introduce a formal framework comprising three components: metacognitive knowledge (self-assessment of capabilities, tasks, and learning strategies), metacognitive planning (deciding what and how to learn), and metacognitive evaluation (reflecting on learning experiences to improve future learning). Analyzing existing self-improving agents, we find they rely predominantly on extrinsic metacognitive mechanisms, which are fixed, human-designed loops that limit scalability and adaptability. Examining each component, we contend that many ingredients for intrinsic metacognition are already present. Finally, we explore how to optimally distribute metacognitive responsibilities between humans and agents, and robustly evaluate and improve intrinsic metacognitive learning, key challenges that must be addressed to enable truly sustained, generalized, and aligned self-improvement.

Methods

The paper formalizes metacognitive learning as a bi-level process. A metacognitive layer sits above the cognitive layer where task-level learning actually happens, monitoring and regulating it. The metacognitive layer has three components that close a loop: knowledge informs planning, planning produces learning activity, and evaluation feeds back into both.

  • Metacognitive knowledge is the agent’s self-model.
    • It comes in three flavors: knowledge of self (what the agent can already do, where its limits lie, what skills it has), knowledge of task (what the current task demands and what would help), and knowledge of strategies (which learning approaches are available and where each tends to apply).
    • The biggest threat to this component is hallucination: LLMs can confidently misrepresent their own internal state, including basic facts about which tools they have access to.
    • The paper cites recent work showing agents can classify math problems by required solution procedure [2] and identify which training tasks would help them, so the ingredient is at least partially present.
  • Metacognitive planning turns that self-model into action through two questions.
    • What to learn is a task-allocation question, traditionally answered by curriculum learning over a curated task pool [3]. Intrinsic variants replace the human-designed curriculum with internal drivers like curiosity, learnability, and regret, and let agents generate their own tasks rather than draw from a fixed pool [4].
    • How to learn is a strategy-selection question with two phases:
      • Exploration (temperature scaling, upper-confidence-bound tree search [5], uncertainty-guided sampling, prompt-based novelty seeking) chooses what experiences the agent gathers.
      • Learning extracts capabilities from those experiences via in-weight updates (finetuning on self-generated traces, à la STaR [6]), long-term memory writes (episodic experiences, abstract rules, reusable skills as tool functions), or both.
    • The paper flags this whole component as the most under-developed in current systems: nearly every shipped agent picks one fixed mechanism and applies it uniformly across tasks and over time.
  • Metacognitive evaluation closes the loop and has two aspects.
    • Tracking progress is the ongoing assessment of how learning is going. Held-out benchmarks like MMLU [7] work for well-defined capabilities. LLM-as-judge [8] fills in for fuzzier targets like emotional intelligence, creativity, or interestingness, where no quantifiable metric exists.
    • Metacognitive reflection is the post-hoc analysis of learning plans, distinct from task-level reflection (Reflexion-style [9]) by operating one level up: it evaluates long-term learning trajectories rather than per-task performance.
    • Because it operates over representations of the cognitive process rather than the task itself, metacognitive reflection can in principle be domain-agnostic, given enough domain-specific signal to extract progress from.

Results

The paper walks three well-known systems through this framework as case studies, ordered by increasing intrinsic-ness:

  • STaR [6] (Zelikman et al., 2022): a reasoning bootstrapping method. Given a small set of problems with reasoning traces plus a larger set with answers only, the agent attempts problems and gets finetuned on any trace that led to a correct answer, then the cycle repeats on harder problems. Almost entirely extrinsic: the agent doesn’t assess its own capabilities, doesn’t choose which tasks to attempt (externally curated), and doesn’t adapt its learning strategy (rationalization with answer hints is fixed). The metacognitive loop sits with the system designer.
  • Voyager [10] (Wang et al., 2023): an LLM-based embodied agent for lifelong learning in Minecraft. It maintains a growing library of executable Python skills and autonomously discovers increasingly complex actions to perform. Partially intrinsic: the agent tracks what it can do (knowledge) and balances exploration against task learnability when picking next goals (planning). The learning strategy stays fixed though: the same exploration-learning loop runs across all tasks. Voyager beats expert-designed curriculum baselines, which the paper takes as evidence the intrinsic components matter.
  • Generative Agents [11] (Park et al., 2023): agents in a Sims-style sandbox that accumulate experiences, form relationships, and develop distinct personas through lived interaction. Most intrinsic of the three. Agents form evolving identities and motivations (knowledge), autonomously plan daily activities (planning), and periodically trigger an abstract reflection, such as recognizing a newfound interest or reinterpreting recent events, that updates their semantic memory and shapes future plans (evaluation). The paper flags the contrast with Reflexion-style [9] techniques: Reflexion reflects at the cognitive level to improve performance on specific tasks; Generative Agents reflect at the metacognitive level, drawing inferences about their own trajectory.

The arc across the three case studies is how the paper builds its argument: each system is intrinsic on more components than the last, and the paper argues the more-intrinsic systems show more sustained progress in the diversity and novelty of their evolving capabilities. The paper acknowledges these are preliminary observations that still require rigorous, systematic studies to substantiate.

My Notes

  • Both limitation claims rest on one example each. The “lose efficacy” claim cites Song et al.’s 2024 generation-verification-gap finding [12]. The “fail to generalize” claim points at STaR and bootstrapped self-training, which worked in their original domain but didn’t transfer. No new experiments.

  • Every shipped agent is extrinsic in this taxonomy. The system designer decides what to monitor, what counts as progress, and when to switch strategies. Supervising Ralph Wiggum [13] hand-designs a Co-Regulation Agent with a fixed role and loop position. ReMA [14] hand-designs the high-low decomposition. The prompt-optimization line (MASS, MetaSPO, EvoPrompt) uses LLMs as inner-loop optimizers but humans fix the search-space structure.

  • “Sustained progress” lacks a cross-system metric. STaR runs in math/reasoning, Voyager in Minecraft, Generative Agents in a Sims sandbox. A residual learning rate (slope late in training over slope early) gets the y-axis unit-free, but the x-axis stays domain-specific: a STaR training step isn’t a Voyager training step, and Sims days don’t align with Minecraft exploration. The cross-system ordering needs either a shared benchmark or a principled x-axis alignment, neither of which the paper provides.

  • SelfReflect bounds the optimism about LLM metacognitive ingredients. The paper argues frontier LLMs already exhibit pieces of metacognitive knowledge, planning, and evaluation. Apple’s SelfReflect [15] finds, across 20 modern models, that LLM self-reports of their own answer distributions don’t match what those models actually sample. So the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient is thinner than the paper’s optimism implies, at least without help from techniques like sample-then-summarize.

item.title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning (NeurIPS 2025) [1], Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, and Sung Ju Hwang (KAIST, DeepAuto.ai) introduce MetaSPO, a bilevel optimization framework that meta-learns a task-agnostic system prompt while simultaneously updating task-specific user prompts in an iterative inner loop.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities, with optimizing their input prompts playing a pivotal role in maximizing their performance. However, while LLM prompts consist of both the task-agnostic system prompts and task-specific user prompts, existing work on prompt optimization has focused on user prompts specific to individual queries or tasks, and largely overlooked the system prompt that is, once optimized, applicable across different tasks and domains. Motivated by this, we introduce the novel problem of bilevel system prompt optimization, whose objective is to design system prompts that are robust to diverse user prompts and transferable to unseen tasks. To tackle this problem, we then propose a meta-learning framework, which meta-learns the system prompt by optimizing it over various user prompts across multiple datasets, while simultaneously updating the user prompts in an iterative manner to ensure synergy between them. We conduct experiments on 14 unseen datasets spanning 5 different domains, on which we show that our approach produces system prompts that generalize effectively to diverse user prompts. Also, our findings reveal that the optimized system prompt enables rapid adaptation even to unseen tasks, requiring fewer optimization steps for test-time user prompts while achieving improved performance.

Methods

Against this three-part structure, MetaSPO’s bilevel algorithm runs two nested optimization loops. The outer loop optimizes the task-agnostic system prompt, and the inner loop iteratively refines task-specific user prompts. At each outer step, the current system prompt is paired with candidate user prompts across multiple source tasks. The model’s failures on held-out examples feed an LLM optimizer that proposes refined candidates (user prompts inside the inner loop, system prompts at the outer loop). The meta-learned system prompt transfers to unseen target tasks with no further system-prompt tuning; at test time, only the user prompt is adapted per target task.

The system prompt starts as “You are a helpful assistant.” (the Default baseline) and is iteratively refined through the outer loop. At each step of either loop, a separate optimizer LLM (GPT-4o mini in the main experiments, distinct from the Llama-3.2 3B base LLM that generates task responses) is prompted with the current prompt and its incorrectly-predicted examples, asked to analyze the failure modes, and then asked for multiple candidate refinements. Candidates are evaluated against held-out task data, and the top-k by performance survive to the next iteration. Both loops follow this same textual-gradient pattern (after Pryzant et al. [4]), applied at different scopes: user prompt per task in the inner loop, system prompt aggregated across source tasks in the outer loop.

Results

The paper evaluates on 14 unseen target tasks across 5 domains (Medical, Review Analysis, Reasoning, Safety, Grounding), with each score the average performance of a system prompt paired with ten different user prompts. Within-domain Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over the 14 tasks, beating the next-best baseline SPRIG at 37.0 and the no-system-prompt Default at 32.2. The cross-domain Global MetaSPO setting (one system prompt meta-learned across all 5 domains) averages 41.4, still ahead of all baselines but ~3 points behind the within-domain Domain setting. Separately, on test-time efficiency: a MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches Default’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation.

Figure 4 tests whether MetaSPO’s lift transfers uniformly across target tasks or depends on source-target task similarity. The paper measures similarity via Bag-of-Words overlap between the source-task training distribution and the target task, then plots per-task improvement against it.

My Notes

  • The contribution is the decomposition, not the method. Before this paper, “prompt optimization” treated the prompt as one optimization target for one task. DSPy [2], MIPRO [3], Pryzant et al.’s textual gradients [4], and EvoPrompt [5] each target a different piece of that setup, but all produce task-specific prompts. The bilevel split (task-agnostic system prompt above, task-specific user prompt below) is the important decision. Once you make it, the meta-learning structure follows naturally because the outer loop has a natural “across tasks” loss to optimize. The MetaSPO algorithm itself is a structurally familiar inner/outer LLM-as-optimizer loop. What matters here is the decision about what to put in each level.
  • The system prompt accounts for most of the transfer.
    • MetaSPO’s headline wins on unseen tasks come from the system prompt. In Table 1’s Unseen Generalization scenario, user prompts are LLM-sampled per task and held fixed; only the system prompt varies across the methods compared. Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over 14 unseen target tasks vs. Default’s 32.2, a +12.3-point lift attributable to the system prompt alone.
    • Appendix B.7 tests system-prompt vs user-prompt optimization head-to-head: MetaSPO (system-prompt optimized on source tasks) vs. ProTeGi (user-prompt optimized on source tasks), evaluated on the unseen Reasoning domain. MetaSPO wins across every source-domain starting point; ProTeGi drops below the Default system prompt, indicating user-prompt optimizations don’t transfer past the specific tasks they were tuned on.
  • A MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches the Default baseline’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation. The headline number is the unseen-generalization performance, but this §4 result is the one that matters for deployment. That’s a recipe for shipping prompt-optimized agents when each new task gets a small calibration budget rather than full re-optimization.
  • Generalization is asymmetric along source-target similarity. Figure 4 shows MetaSPO’s gain over Default scales with source-target task similarity measured by Bag-of-Words. High similarity, big gain; low similarity, the meta-learned system prompt is closer to neutral. That’s the expected meta-learning failure mode on out-of-distribution tasks, but it also bounds the deployment story: a system prompt meta-learned on Medical+Review+Reasoning will help most on tasks that look like those at the BoW level, and the cross-domain Global setting underperforms the within-domain Domain setting (41.4 vs. 44.5 avg). The follow-up question: at what point does the meta-learned prior become a liability on a sufficiently distant task?

  2. Khattab, O., Singhvi, A., Maheshwari, P., Zhang, Z., Santhanam, K., Vardhamanan, S., Haq, S., Sharma, A., Joshi, T.
